batch: BATCH 1 gaps, time and the sampler model

findings.title: The fixed 30 s gap rule zeroes all CPU at cadences the settings accept, and `submeter top --seconds 31..60` prints zeros
findings.evidence: sampler.py:39 gap_after_s=30.0; :55 gap = elapsed > gap_after_s or wall-elapsed > 2; :67 cpu_busy_s=0.0 if gap; :78-79 every process cpu_s=0.0. config.py:46-51 idle 1s-60s, cold 5s-60s; :92 on_battery_multiplier up to 10; no gap setting. docs/08:70-71 multiplier stretches every interval; overhead guard lengthens intervals (docs/17:230). cli.py:79 top max=60.0, :87 Sampler() default. docs/14:244 states the fixed 30 s rule. docs/17:75 'a change of cadence never loses or invents CPU time'. verify-1/gap_rule.out.txt: part 1 'idle 60s x on_battery_multiplier 10  accepted; 600.0 s between samples'; part 2 '29 s: gap=False ... credited 14.5' vs '31 s: gap=True, process used 15.5 CPU-s, credited 0.0; machine busy recorded 0.0'; part 3 'top --seconds 2 ... CPU-s summed 0.470' vs '--seconds 31 ... 448 processes, interval_s 31.1, CPU-s summed 0.000'.
findings.impact: Any interval over 30 s, whether set in the config, stretched by the battery multiplier or lengthened by the overhead guard, records zero CPU for every workload and zero machine busy time. Attribution totals, trends and the reconciliation read zero while the machine is busy. The documented `top` command prints 0.00 cores for every workload when --seconds is 31 to 60. A stall in which both clocks keep running also loses its CPU, although it is not a suspend.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py: ingest() takes the expected interval for this tick. A tick is a gap only when elapsed > 3 x expected + slack, or when the suspend test fires (see G9). Do not zero CPU or I/O deltas in a gap batch: the counters are cumulative, so the deltas are exact, and a suspended process accrues nothing. The flag controls coverage only (G2). src/submeter/cli.py top: pass --seconds as the expected interval. docs/14:244 and docs/05 step 3: state the rule. Tests: a 60 s interval is not a gap; a 35 s stall at a 1 s cadence is a gap that keeps its CPU. Second problem, from C-storage#2: rollup.py:110 puts a sample whole in the bucket that holds its midpoint, so once 60-600 s samples are legal, roll_up must split a sample across bucket edges in proportion to time, and docs/17:123 finality must be at least the longest interval.
findings.cost: About 15 lines in sampler.py and cli.py, 2 tests, a sentence each in docs/05 and docs/14. The proportional split in rollup.py is about 15 more lines.
findings.verification: I re-read sampler.py:39-69, config.py:43-92, cli.py:77-105 and docs/08:57-71, and found no gap setting, no caller that passes gap_after_s, and no cross-validation of the intervals. I wrote verify-1/gap_rule.py, which feeds the real load_settings and Sampler and runs the real `top` through typer's CliRunner, with sleep replaced by a clock offset so nothing was re-timed. The results match the leads exactly, including a 29 s vs 31 s boundary that the leads did not show. Refutation attempt: the collector loop is not built, so a builder could pass a larger gap_after_s. But docs/14:244 states 30 s as fixed behaviour and nothing ties it to cadence, and `top` is shipped baseline code that is wrong today, so critical stands. The cluster holds a second, distinct problem (C-storage#2 part 3: samples of 60 s or more overflow minute buckets and arrive after finality). I verified it by reading rollup.py:110 and kept it as a secondary note under the main finding.

findings.title: A gap is stored and rolled up as covered zero-use time: one minute bucket claims 3601 covered seconds and the hour passes well_covered
findings.evidence: sampler.py:59 gives a gap batch interval_s=max(elapsed, wall). rules.py:219-221 copies batch.interval_s into every WorkloadSample, which has no gap field (models.py:135-147). raw.py:97-129 writes the gap row AND the system_raw and workload_raw rows for the gap batch. rollup.py:49-53,60,68-71 add the interval to covered_s, the memory mean, active_s and both histograms. :110 puts the sample in the bucket that holds its midpoint. :171-173 well_covered means covered >= 0.5 x width. verify-1/gap_rule.out.txt part 4 (real Sampler, aggregate, RawFile, roll_up; 2.00 cores, 1 h suspend): 'batch interval_s 3601, workload row interval_s [3601.0]'; 'minute bucket at +2400 s: covered_s 3601 of 60, cpu_s 0, well_covered True'; 'hour bucket at +0 s: covered_s 4201, cpu_s 1200, mean cores 0.29, well_covered True' (truth: observed 600 s at 2.00 cores). docs/06:38 and docs/17:120 say covered seconds exist 'so a gap is never read as zero use'.
findings.impact: After every sleep, one minute bucket claims more coverage than its width with zero use. The hour that holds it reads 0.29 cores instead of 2.00, and it passes well_covered, so baselines, the slow-growth check and trends take sleep as idle use (docs/06:102, docs/17:132). system_raw is stored the same way, so the machine busy share is understated too (C-storage#1 measured 12.5% vs 50%). The fixes listed for R08 and R24 are not present in the baseline.
findings.proposed_change: core/models.py: add gap: bool to WorkloadSample. attribution/rules.py aggregate(): pass batch.gap. store/rollup.py SeriesAccumulator.add(): for a gap sample, add cpu_s, I/O and started to the sums, but add nothing to covered_s, samples, active_s, the memory weight or either histogram. Reject a non-gap sample whose interval_s exceeds width_s. store/raw.py: store the flag (a gap column on workload_raw and system_raw), and have workload_samples() return it. Test: Sampler to bucket across a suspend gives covered_s <= width_s and well_covered False. Do not use C-storage#1's interval_s=0 variant: rollup.py:50 drops a row with interval 0 whole, which would lose the CPU that G1's fix keeps.
findings.cost: About 15 changed lines in four modules, plus one test
findings.verification: I re-read every cited line and grepped src/ for any reader of the gap table: only raw.py writes it, and nothing subtracts it from coverage. tests/test_baseline.py:404-418 checks only that a gap row exists. I drove the full chain myself in verify-1/gap_rule.py part 4 and got the same 3601-of-60 minute and a well-covered hour. Searched docs/05, 06, 14 and 17: docs/14:298 says only that a gap batch is written in full. The verdict is 'with changes' because one lead's fix (interval_s 0) conflicts with G1's fix, so I chose the gap-flag form that two of the three leads proposed.

findings.title: The hot and cold sets cannot be built on the sampler as designed: cold CPU is lost and exits and starts are invented, or the cold CPU lands as 10x spikes
findings.evidence: sampler.py:47-49 keeps only the last snapshot; :65 calls everything absent 'exited'; :84-87 credits 0 to an old process seen again; :104-112 hot_keys() is documented as 'Processes worth sampling at the active interval'. models.py:122-132 has one interval_s per batch. docs/05:45 'the hot set every 1 s and the cold set every 10 s'; docs/08:61,63; docs/17:71; R02. Nothing says which fields the cold set skips. verify-1/hot_cold.out.txt (1 hot process at 0.90 cores, 9 cold at 0.02, 30 ticks): 'A: ... cold credited 0.00 of 5.40; exits reported 27, starts reported 27 (truth 0 and 0)'; 'B: ... cold credited 5.40 of 5.40 ...; cold set's highest one-tick rate 1.80 cores (truth 0.18)'.
findings.impact: Build-list item 3 has two possible readings, and both give wrong numbers on the existing sampler. Partial snapshots lose all cold-set CPU and inflate the started count, which is a cost metric. Carrying cold counters forward keeps the totals but puts 10 s of CPU into a 1 s interval, which corrupts per-tick cores, percentiles and spike detection. The phase-1 gate 'totals reconcile within 2%' would fail under the first reading.
findings.proposed_change: Decision first. Under option (a): docs/05 step 2, docs/17:71 and the docs/08 rows for active_interval and cold_interval should say that every tick reads cumulative CPU, memory and I/O for every process (the Windows bulk call returns them all), and that the hot and cold sets decide only which costly extras are read (USS, handles, working folder, command line). Reword the sampler.py hot_keys() docstring to match. Under option (b): Snapshot gains complete: bool, ProcessSample gains its own interval_s, and the Sampler keeps the last counters of processes absent from a partial snapshot.
findings.cost: (a): about four sentences in three docs and one docstring. (b): about 30 lines in models.py and sampler.py, plus tests.
findings.decision_question: Do the hot and cold sets decide (a) which costly per-process extras are read, with CPU, memory and I/O read for every process every tick, or (b) which processes appear in a snapshot at all, with per-process intervals added to the model? Recommendation: (a). The Windows bulk snapshot returns every process anyway, and (a) keeps one interval per batch and the sampler unchanged.
findings.verification: I re-read the sampler and models, and I searched docs/05, 08, 14 and 17 and R02 for which fields a cold read skips: none says. I wrote verify-1/hot_cold.py, which feeds the real Sampler both ways, and reproduced both failure modes on a smaller synthetic set. I downgraded severity from critical (B) to high: the numbers are wrong only once someone builds the cold set on this sampler, the design is silent rather than wrong, and the phase-1 reconcile gate would catch reading (b). I did not re-time the /proc stat-only read cost that B cites for option (a), so that figure is the lead's.

findings.title: A wall-clock step back reopens a closed day file, packs 90 covered seconds into a minute and delays keyframes; a step forward discards an observed interval
findings.evidence: sampler.py:55 marks a gap only when wall runs ahead of monotonic. :58 taken_at is the raw wall time. raw.py:265-274 opens any day that differs from the current one. :275-278 makes a keyframe due on the difference of taken_at values. docs/17:112 'A closed day's file is never written again'. verify-1/clock_step.out.txt (sub-millisecond jitter on every tick): 'back-30s: true CPU 120 s; ... stored CPU 120; gap batches 0; batches stamped earlier than the one before 1; fullest minute covered_s 90 of 60'; 'back-50s-midnight: ... files written in order [2026-11-20.db, 2026-11-21.db, 2026-11-20.db, 2026-11-21.db]'; 'forward-5s: true CPU 120 s; sampler credited 119; ... gap batches 1'.
findings.impact: After a backward step (an NTP step, a manual change, dual boot), timestamps go backwards. One minute bucket claims more coverage than its width, a closed day file is written again, and the next keyframe waits an extra S seconds beyond R31's 10 minutes. Nothing records the step, so no epoch explains the dip. A forward step of more than 2 s turns an observed 1 s interval into a 6 s gap with zero CPU. CPU totals survive a backward step when timestamps carry real sub-second values.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py: set taken_at = anchor wall time + monotonic elapsed. When the wall clock departs from that by more than the slack and the suspend test (G9) does not fire, re-anchor and emit a 'clock stepped' event that starts an epoch (R32), not a gap. taken_at never decreases. src/submeter/store/raw.py RawStore.write: never reopen a day earlier than the open file. docs/14:244 and docs/17 Collection: one sentence on clock steps. Tests: a step back and a step forward.
findings.cost: About 20 lines in sampler.py and raw.py, plus two tests
findings.verification: I re-read sampler.py:53-59 and raw.py:97-129 and 259-282. The lead's headline, 'silently overwrites stored samples', comes from whole-second synthetic ticks, which collide under INSERT OR REPLACE. C-storage#4 itself found no loss with a 30.25 s step. My probe verify-1/clock_step.py adds sub-millisecond jitter, as time.time() has, and found no rows lost and stored CPU 120 of 120 after a 30 s step back. What remains, all reproduced: non-monotonic timestamps, a 90-of-60 minute, a reopened closed day, and a forward step that drops 1 CPU-s and records a gap. The keyframe delay I verified by reading raw.py:275-278, not by running it. I downgraded severity from high (C) to medium: the totals survive, and the trigger, a clock step, is uncommon. How often Windows steps rather than slews is not verified here.

findings.title: ProcessKey.started is a wall-clock float derived from btime, so a clock step cuts children from their parent's workload and an uncached reader re-keys every process
findings.evidence: psutil/_pslinux.py:1849-1863 create_time = cached ticks/CLOCK_TICKS + boot_time() ('This is subject to system clock updates'). :1507-1515 boot_time() reads /proc/stat btime on every call. psutil/__init__.py:390-394 makes psutil's own Linux identity create_time(monotonic=True) 'since it is stable over changes to system time'. :776-781 create_time is cached per object and 'may be affected by ... NTP'. psutil_provider.py:57 uses the wall form. rules.py:145-148 rejects a parent that started after the child. sampler.py:84 runs the born-this-interval test on wall time. verify-1/start_time.out.txt: 'same process, two fresh objects: start times differ by 1.000 s'; 'child start minus parent start -3600 s; parent -> 'probe', child -> 'unattributed' (no rule matched)'; 'no cache: ... 456 processes; first_seen 456; reported exited 456; CPU credited 0.000 s, machine busy 0.460 s'.
findings.impact: After a backward step of S seconds, every child born within S seconds of its cached parent's start loses the include_children rule and stays unattributed for the parent's lifetime, so attribution fails for a freshly started agent. A provider that does not cache start times re-keys every process whenever btime moves by one second: all processes exit and restart, one interval's CPU is lost, and the process table duplicates (R25). The /proc reader of docs/17:71 is such a provider, and so is a switch to the psutil fallback (R17) if the two compute the float differently.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17:77: 'The start time in a process identity is the platform's integer stamp: on Linux, field 22 of /proc/PID/stat (ticks since boot) with /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id; on Windows, CreateTime as a FILETIME integer. Convert to wall time only for display. Compare start times, and test whether a process was born in an interval, on the boot clock.' Baseline: models.py ProcessKey.started becomes an int; psutil_provider.py:57 uses the boot-relative value on Linux; Snapshot carries a boot-clock reading for sampler.py:84; raw.py process and process_raw get INTEGER columns. Windows CreateTime is system time at creation, so a backward step there still inverts parent order; record step events (G4) and state this in known limits.
findings.cost: One sentence in docs/17, and about 30 lines across models.py, psutil_provider.py, sampler.py and raw.py, plus a test
findings.verification: I re-read psutil 7.2.2 source in .venv and confirmed that btime is re-read on every create_time() of a new object, and that psutil itself avoids the wall form for identity. I wrote verify-1/start_time.py with a simulated step (psutil's boot_time replaced in-process; the real clock was untouched). It reproduced the parent rejection through the real provider, Sampler and Attributor, and the re-keying of all processes with an uncached reader. Refutation: the psutil provider's per-object cache protects processes already seen, so re-keying needs an uncached provider (the planned /proc reader) or a provider switch. Parent rejection affects only children born within S seconds of the parent's start. A float mismatch between a Windows bulk provider and psutil is plausible but not verified here. Severity: E said high, A-linux said medium. I chose medium because steps are uncommon and the effect is bounded.

findings.title: A pid reused while psutil's process_iter cache holds the old process is missing from two snapshots, then credited no CPU
findings.evidence: psutil/__init__.py:625-650 is_running() marks the pid reused and raises NoSuchProcess. :666 ppid() calls _raise_if_pid_reused() on every OS. :1540-1550 process_iter() removes the reused pid after computing new_pids, so the next pass skips it as well. psutil_provider.py:91 calls ppid(); :102-103 turns NoSuchProcess into None. verify-1/pid_reuse.out.txt (reuse imitated as psutil's tests do): 'snapshot 1: pid missing from the snapshot' / 'snapshot 2: pid missing from the snapshot' / 'snapshot 3: present, first_seen True, born 4.9 s before this snapshot, credited 0.00 CPU-s'.
findings.impact: For the psutil provider, a process that takes a reused pid is in no bucket for two ticks, and its first seconds of CPU are never credited, against 'never dropped' (docs/17:78). This is rare on Linux (pid_max 4194304). It matters mainly where psutil is the required Windows fallback (R17); how fast Windows reuses pids is not verified here.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/providers/psutil_provider.py: when a pid that psutil.pids() still lists raises NoSuchProcess, read it again in the same tick through a fresh psutil.Process(pid). Add a test that ages the cached object as verify-1/pid_reuse.py does.
findings.verification: I re-read the psutil 7.2.2 paths and wrote my own probe (a `sleep 6` child; its cached object given an older identity and start time; snapshots 1.1 s apart, so the born-this-interval test sees a real cadence). It reproduced the two missing snapshots and a zero credit. The reuse is imitated, not produced, but the code path is real psutil. I kept severity low and moved the disposition from fix now to plan: the change belongs with the phase-1 provider fallback work (R17), and nothing in planning depends on it.

findings.title: A stand-in zero CPU counter becomes the next delta's baseline, crediting a process's whole lifetime of CPU to one interval
findings.evidence: psutil_provider.py:65-66 sets cpu_s 0.0 and restricted True on AccessDenied. :104-110 sets started=0.0 on outer AccessDenied. sampler.py:80-81 subtracts before.cpu_s with no check and no upper bound. verify-1/zero_baseline.out.txt: 'cpu stand-in: interval 1 s, first_seen False, credited 5000 CPU-s on a 4-core machine'; 'start-time stand-in: exited 1, first_seen True, credited 0 CPU-s'. How often it fires, on this machine as an ordinary user: '453 processes: create_time 0, cpu_times 0, memory_info 0, num_threads 0, io_counters 298, cmdline 0'. psutil _pswindows.py:937-946 (cpu_times), :789-803 (memory_info) and :913-921 (create_time) fall back to NtQuerySystemInformation on a permission error.
findings.impact: When the flip happens, one workload is credited thousands of CPU-seconds in a single 1 s interval, which is impossible on the machine and wrong in every total and percentile. With psutil the stand-in path is close to unreachable: no refusals here, and fallbacks on Windows. It needs hidepid mounts with a process that changes credentials, or a future provider that writes stand-in zeros. The module whose stated job is to stop invented CPU has no guard against it.
findings.proposed_change: core/models.py: ProcessCounters.cpu_s becomes float | None, None meaning unreadable. providers/psutil_provider.py: write None, not 0.0, and never write started=0.0. collector/sampler.py: a None on either side gives no CPU baseline (credit 0, as for an old first sighting). Cap every per-process delta at interval_s x logical_cores and count the capped samples. Do not key this on before.restricted: io_counters refusal alone marks 298 of 453 processes restricted here, so that test would stop crediting CPU to most system processes.
findings.verification: I reproduced the 5000 CPU-s credit with the real Sampler. To test how often it happens, I counted AccessDenied per psutil call over every process on this machine: zero for every call that feeds the stand-in. I read psutil's Windows fallbacks in .venv. I downgraded severity from high to medium because the code path is certain but no real trigger was shown with the shipped provider. I changed the fix after finding that `restricted` is set by io_counters alone on two-thirds of the processes, which makes the lead's restricted-based test unsafe.

findings.title: One process's unexpected read error aborts the whole snapshot, and zombies are dropped although their CPU is readable
findings.evidence: psutil_provider.py:76-82 catches only AccessDenied and NotImplementedError on io_counters. :44 has no per-process guard. :102-103 maps ZombieProcess to None. psutil/_pslinux.py:1808-1825 raises RuntimeError for an empty /proc/PID/io and ValueError for a missing field. :1584-1607 wrap_exceptions re-raises FileNotFoundError when stat still exists. :1790 defines io_counters only if /proc/self/io exists. verify-1/read_errors.out.txt: 'RuntimeError: snapshot() raised RuntimeError', the same for ValueError and OSError; real zombie: 'cpu_times: ok', 'cmdline: ZombieProcess', 'in PsutilProvider().snapshot(): False'.
findings.impact: A single malformed /proc entry costs the whole tick, or crashes the collector if the loop does not catch it, against 'never dropped' (docs/17:78). How often it fires is unknown. A zombie's final CPU, which is readable, is discarded; that hits the short-lived children polling most needs (R01).
findings.proposed_change: providers/psutil_provider.py: each optional read (io_counters, cmdline, cwd) catches psutil.Error, OSError, RuntimeError and ValueError and leaves that field None, marking the process partial. ZombieProcess raised by cmdline or cwd keeps the record with its CPU. Wrap _read so that one process failing yields a restricted record, not an aborted snapshot. Note for the child-time recovery in docs/17:71: a zombie counted here must not be counted again from the parent's cutime after reaping.
findings.verification: I re-read the provider and psutil's Linux paths. My probe verify-1/read_errors.py patched io_counters for one child, and each of the three exceptions escaped snapshot(). It then created a real zombie: cmdline is the call that raises ZombieProcess, while create_time, cpu_times, memory_info, num_threads, ppid and name succeed. io_counters exists only where /proc/PID/io exists, so a kernel without I/O accounting is not a trigger; the trigger frequency stays unknown, hence medium rather than high.

findings.title: On Windows the monotonic clock counts sleep, so suspend detection rests only on the 30 s rule, and the documented check for it cannot fail
findings.evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/acquiring-high-resolution-time-stamps: 'QueryPerformanceCounter reads the performance counter and returns the total number of ticks that have occurred since the Windows operating system was started, including the time when the machine was in a sleep state such as standby, hibernate, or connected standby.' https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.13.html: 'On Windows, monotonic() now uses the QueryPerformanceCounter() clock ...'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/realtimeapiset/nf-realtimeapiset-queryunbiasedinterrupttime: 'The unbiased interrupt-time count does not include time the system spends in sleep or hibernation.' sampler.py:55. docs/reference/windows-priorities.md:69 lists this as unknown and says 'Either answer produces a gap, by a different rule'. :70 check: 'start uv run submeter top --seconds 60, put the computer to sleep for a minute inside that window, and confirm the result reports no burst of CPU time'. verify-1/gap_rule.out.txt part 3: '--seconds 60, no sleep ... CPU-s summed 0.000', and 0.000 again with 40 s asleep under either clock behaviour.
findings.impact: On Windows with Python 3.13 or later, wall minus monotonic stays near 0 across a suspend. Only the 30 s rule marks it, so a suspend under 30 s is counted as observed time. G1's fix also cannot tell a stall from a suspend using these two clocks. The phase-0 check gives false assurance: `top --seconds 60` is always a gap and always prints zero CPU, whatever the clock does.
findings.proposed_change: docs/reference/windows-priorities.md section 5: replace the 'unknown' with the Microsoft sentence, and replace the check with one that can fail (run a 10 s expected interval across a 60 s sleep and print gap and interval_s). docs/17 'Detect suspend and resume': 'Suspend is the growth of a clock that counts sleep over one that does not: CLOCK_BOOTTIME minus CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Linux, QueryPerformanceCounter minus QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime on Windows. Neither needs administrator rights.' Snapshot carries both readings; the sampler code is part of G1's change.
findings.cost: Three sentences now. About 10 lines in the provider and sampler with G1, plus a Windows check in P0.
findings.verification: The lead was suspected because it could not find vendor text. I fetched Microsoft's high-resolution time stamps page and found the sentence that settles it (QPC includes standby, hibernate and connected standby). I also re-fetched the Python 3.13 note that monotonic() uses QPC, and the QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime page as the sleep-excluding counterpart, which runs in user mode and fits fixed rule 2. Running the real `top` through CliRunner showed that the windows-priorities.md check reports zero CPU in every case, so it cannot detect anything. I raised status to verified and severity from low to medium, because the documented check is misleading and the defect constrains G1's fix. The CPU deltas themselves stay exact, so it is not high.

findings.title: The design names Python 3.12, whose time.monotonic() on Windows steps in 15.6 ms, too coarse for 250 ms intervals
findings.evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.13.html: 'On Windows, monotonic() now uses the QueryPerformanceCounter() clock for a resolution of 1 microsecond, instead of the GetTickCount64() clock which has a resolution of 15.6 milliseconds.' pyproject.toml:5 requires-python '>=3.12'. docs/11:5 'Recommended: Python 3.12 for all of version 1'. docs/01:26 'Python 3.12 throughout'. docs/17:36 'Python 3.12 or newer'. config.py:44 active_interval down to 250ms. psutil_provider.py:43 time.monotonic(); sampler.py:53 interval from its difference.
findings.impact: On Windows with 3.12, each interval length carries up to ±15.6 ms of error: ±6% on a 250 ms interval and ±1.6% at the 1 s default. That noise goes into per-tick rates and the cores histogram. Totals are unaffected because the intervals telescope. The design explicitly recommends 3.12, so a builder following docs/11 gets this.
findings.proposed_change: pyproject.toml: requires-python '>=3.13'. docs/17:36, docs/01:26 and docs/11:5: name Python 3.13. docs/reference/windows-priorities.md:28 and :68: update to match.
findings.verification: I re-fetched the Python 3.13 What's New text and the quote is exact. I re-read pyproject and found that the design documents name 3.12 outright, which makes this more likely than the lead stated; this checkout resolves 3.14.5. Nothing was re-timed. I downgraded severity from medium to low: the error is per-sample noise at short cadences, totals are exact, and Windows per-process CPU times may themselves be tick-granular (not verified here), so 3.13 removes one noise source but perhaps not all.
